strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: monocular 4D human-scene reconstruction in unconstrained videos, combining global SMPL motion, camera poses, and dense scene geometry rather than treating them as separate outputs.
The core idea of using human-scene contact as a bridge between scale/camera/scene optimization and global human motion is well motivated and practically useful.
Empirical results are strong across EMDB, SLOPER4D, and RICH, with clear improvements over strong human-motion and scene-reconstruction baselines on both motion metrics and scene/camera metrics.

Ablations support the main technical claim: contact scale constraints provide a large gain, joint optimization improves human motion further, and the final formulation incrementally improves reconstruction quality.

The paper includes an efficient JOSH3R variant and shows that pseudo-labels from the optimization method can train a faster model, which is a useful direction for scaling annotation of in-the-wild videos.
The manuscript is generally clear, well structured, and provides enough implementation detail to understand the optimization procedure and major design choices.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate rather than high: the method largely combines strong existing components, MASt3R/MASt3R-SfM, human mesh recovery, segmentation, and contact prediction, with relatively simple contact losses and gradient-based refinement.

The contact correspondence construction is heuristic and may be brittle under occlusion, incorrect masks, wrong contact predictions, non-static contacts, soft/deformable surfaces, or cases where the closest projected scene point is not the actual contact point. The paper acknowledges some limitations but does not deeply quantify these failure modes.

The evaluation of true 4D human-scene reconstruction remains indirect. Since no direct baseline exists, the paper evaluates human motion and scene reconstruction separately, which does not fully measure interaction coherence, contact correctness, penetration, sliding, or physical plausibility.

Dataset coverage is somewhat narrow: SLOPER4D has only 6 public sequences, RICH is a selected subset, and JOSH3R is evaluated mainly where its pseudo-label training distribution is most similar. This leaves uncertainty about generalization to diverse web videos, indoor scenes, seated/lying motions, object interactions, crowds, and low-quality footage.

The JOSH3R results are useful for efficiency but substantially weaker than JOSH and only modestly better than optimization-free baselines; the claim of strong generalization from pseudo-labels is only partially supported.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on multiple large external models and unstated engineering details around segmentation/tracking failures, multi-person association, sequence concatenation, hyperparameter sensitivity, and pseudo-label filtering. Runtime is also slow for JOSH at 0.8 FPS despite being framed as a scalable annotation tool.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and difficult problem: monocular 4D human-scene reconstruction in unconstrained videos, with an appealing goal of jointly estimating global human motion, camera poses, and dense scene geometry rather than treating them as independent outputs.

The core contact-based optimization idea is intuitive and potentially useful: using human-scene contact to resolve scale, reduce sliding, and tie scene geometry to global motion is a sensible constraint for this setting.

The paper reports consistent numerical improvements for JOSH over constructed baselines on EMDB, SLOPER4D, and RICH, including both human motion metrics and scene/camera reconstruction metrics where available.
The ablation study supports the importance of the contact scale loss and joint optimization, especially on SLOPER4D, where large gains appear when contact constraints are introduced.
The inclusion of JOSH3R recognizes the practical cost of iterative optimization and attempts to distill the pipeline into a faster model trained from pseudo-labels.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Much of the system is a composition of existing strong components, especially MASt3R/MASt3R-SfM for scene reconstruction, existing human mesh recovery, video segmentation, and contact prediction. The main new contribution is a relatively simple contact-based optimization objective and a lightweight prediction head.

The evaluation does not convincingly validate the full claimed task of 4D human-scene reconstruction. The paper mostly evaluates human motion and scene reconstruction separately, with limited direct measurement of human-scene interaction quality, contact correctness, physical plausibility, or temporal consistency beyond proxy metrics.

The baselines are largely constructed by the authors rather than being established methods for the exact task, which makes the strength of the comparisons difficult to judge. Some baselines may be disadvantaged by ad hoc scale recovery or by not being tuned for the same contact/metric-scale setting.

JOSH3R is weakly supported. It is trained on pseudo-labels from JOSH and evaluated mainly on SLOPER4D-like pedestrian urban motion; its EMDB result in the appendix is far worse than several existing methods. This undercuts the claim of broad generalization and makes the real-time variant feel preliminary.

The method depends on many predicted intermediate quantities, including segmentation masks, local SMPL estimates, contact labels, scene correspondences, and visibility heuristics. The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure modes or sensitivity to errors in these components.

The contact correspondence heuristic is fragile: nearest projected scene point for predicted contact vertices can be unreliable under occlusion, sparse/noisy geometry, incorrect masks, non-ground contacts, or ambiguous image projections. The paper acknowledges some limitations but does not quantify them.

The experimental scope is narrow relative to the claims. SLOPER4D has only six public sequences, RICH evaluation uses a subset, and the web-video pseudo-label set is relatively small and domain-specific despite being used to argue in-the-wild generalization.

There are presentation and consistency issues that reduce confidence, such as unclear/inconsistent optimization details in the appendix and differing JOSH numbers across tables. The paper would benefit from clearer reproducibility details, runtime breakdowns, and component-level error analysis.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: monocular 4D human-scene reconstruction in unconstrained videos, jointly recovering global human motion, camera trajectory, and dense scene geometry rather than treating them as separate outputs.

The central idea of using human-scene contact as a bridge between global human motion estimation and metric scene reconstruction is well motivated and technically sensible. The contact scale and contact static losses provide a clear mechanism for resolving scale and reducing physically implausible motion such as foot sliding.

The empirical results are strong across several relevant datasets. JOSH improves global human motion estimation on EMDB, SLOPER4D, and RICH, and also improves metric-scale scene reconstruction metrics over reasonable combinations of recent scene and motion methods.

The ablation study on SLOPER4D is useful and supports the main claim that contact-guided joint optimization improves both scene and human estimates. The improvement from no optimization to contact-based scene optimization is especially convincing.

The JOSH3R variant is a valuable practical addition: it addresses the runtime cost of iterative optimization and demonstrates that JOSH can generate useful pseudo-labels for training an optimization-free model.
The paper is generally clear, well structured, and positioned against relevant work in global human motion estimation, dense reconstruction, and human-scene interaction.
weaknesses: The method depends heavily on several off-the-shelf components, including MASt3R/MASt3R-SfM, camera-frame human mesh recovery, video segmentation, and contact prediction. Failure modes from these components are acknowledged but not deeply quantified, making robustness in difficult in-the-wild settings less certain.

The contact correspondence construction is heuristic and assumes visible, reliable human-scene contacts. This is plausible for walking and hand/foot contact, but the paper gives limited analysis of cases with occlusion, intermittent contact, soft contact, non-contact actions, clutter, or incorrect contact labels.

The evaluation is strong but still somewhat constrained. SLOPER4D has only six public sequences, RICH uses a subset of 40 moving-camera sequences, and JOSH3R is mainly validated on urban pedestrian-like motion similar to its pseudo-label training data.

The baselines are necessarily assembled because no prior method directly solves the same task, but this makes comparisons somewhat fragile. Performance may depend on implementation choices for combining scene reconstruction with human mesh recovery and scale recovery.

The paper would benefit from more explicit reproducibility details: release plans, runtime/memory beyond FPS, exact hyperparameters for all loss weights, and clarification of the apparent appendix typo where the second optimization stage says it uses the 2D projection loss while setting w2D = 0.

The segment-wise evaluation and alignment protocol should be discussed more carefully, since splitting into 100-frame windows and aligning segments can hide long-horizon drift, which is especially relevant for global trajectory reconstruction.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: monocular 4D human-scene reconstruction in unconstrained videos, including camera pose, dense scene geometry, and global multi-human motion.

The core idea of using human-scene contact as a bridge for joint optimization is intuitive, well motivated, and produces coherent improvements across human motion, scene reconstruction, and physical plausibility metrics.
The method is modular and can use different human mesh and scene reconstruction initializers, which strengthens the practical value of the framework.
The empirical results are broad relative to the task, with evaluations on SLOPER4D, EMDB, and RICH, plus ablations for contact losses, local human optimization, and focal-length optimization.

The paper includes useful analysis of pseudo-labeling web videos and training an end-to-end JOSH3R model, suggesting a plausible path from optimization-based reconstruction to scalable learned systems.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the contribution is mainly a carefully engineered joint optimization framework combining existing human recovery, scene reconstruction, contact prediction, segmentation, and robust losses, rather than a fundamentally new model or learning principle.

The strongest 4D reconstruction comparison depends on a reimplementation of SynCHMR because the original code is unavailable, making the fairness and fidelity of the main baseline difficult to verify.

Some headline gains are partly confounded by stronger initializers. Although counterpart comparisons are provided, comparisons such as JOSH3 versus SynCHMR mix joint optimization with substantially different human and scene initialization quality.

The evaluation scale is still limited for the central 4D reconstruction claim: SLOPER4D has only six public sequences, and the scene reconstruction evaluation excludes a hard sequence where all methods fail, which may overstate robustness.

The method relies heavily on off-the-shelf contact prediction, segmentation, monocular depth, and visible contact correspondences. Failure modes with no contact, occluded contact, incorrect contact labels, or severe dynamic background are acknowledged but not deeply evaluated.

The pseudo-labeling/JOSH3R results are promising but not yet compelling as a major contribution: JOSH3R is faster but substantially less accurate than JOSH and underperforms strong baselines on EMDB and RICH, with gains mainly on SLOPER4D-like pedestrian data.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the abstract has an unfinished code/model availability statement, and the full pipeline depends on many external components and grid-searched hyperparameters.

The ethical discussion around web videos is too high level; “remove all personally identifiable information” is not operationally specified despite the work reconstructing human motion from public footage.

strengths: The paper targets an important and challenging problem: joint reconstruction of human motion, camera motion, and scene geometry from monocular in-the-wild videos.
The core intuition that human-scene contact can couple otherwise separate human and scene optimization is reasonable and technically plausible.
The method is evaluated across several relevant benchmarks and metrics, including human motion accuracy, scene reconstruction, camera trajectory, and physical plausibility metrics.
The ablations suggest that the contact scene loss, contact static loss, and focal length optimization each contribute to performance, at least under the reported setup.
weaknesses: The experimental case is substantially weakened by confounded comparisons. The strongest results compare JOSH variants using much stronger initializers against baselines with different or older initializations, so the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed joint optimization.

The main 4D reconstruction baseline, SynCHMR, is reimplemented because the original code is unavailable. This makes the central comparison fragile, especially since the paper does not provide enough validation that the reimplementation is faithful or competitive.

The evaluation scale is limited for such broad claims. SLOPER4D has only 6 public sequences, and the paper excludes a difficult sequence from scene reconstruction evaluation because all methods fail, which biases the reported scene results upward and weakens the in-the-wild robustness claim.

The method depends heavily on many off-the-shelf components: human mesh recovery, segmentation, contact prediction, depth/point maps, correspondences, and pose estimation. Failure modes and sensitivity to realistic correlated errors from these modules are not sufficiently characterized.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. Joint optimization with contact, smoothness, reprojection, and scene correspondence losses is a natural extension of existing human-scene and human-camera optimization pipelines, and the paper does not clearly establish a fundamentally new formulation.

Several claims are overstated. In particular, claims about scalable pseudo-labeling and robust web-video generalization are supported mostly by limited downstream experiments, while JOSH3R remains substantially worse than JOSH and often worse than strong global motion baselines on accuracy.

The contact constraints rely on predicted contact labels and visible contact correspondences, which are exactly unreliable in many in-the-wild settings. The paper acknowledges this limitation but does not adequately quantify how often contact is absent, occluded, or incorrectly inferred.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the abstract says code/model are available but the reproducibility statement says release will occur upon publication, and the web-video pseudo-label dataset does not appear to be released or specified in enough detail for replication.

The ethics discussion is too shallow for reconstructing pedestrians from YouTube videos. The claim that footage is non-identifiable is not well substantiated, and risks around surveillance-like downstream use are noted but not meaningfully mitigated.

The paper has presentation and polish issues, including typos, inconsistent wording, some confusing metric labels, and at least one appendix section that incorrectly says it provides more global human motion results while discussing dense scene reconstruction.

strengths: Clear and meaningful contribution: the paper formulates monocular 4D human-scene reconstruction as a joint optimization over camera poses, scene geometry, and multi-human global motion, using human-scene contact as the coupling signal. This is a well-motivated advance over sequential pipelines.

The method is technically sensible and modular. JOSH can use different human mesh recovery and scene reconstruction initializers, which makes the contribution more general than a single tightly coupled pipeline.

Empirical results are strong across several axes: global human motion, dense scene reconstruction, camera trajectory, and physical plausibility. The gains over matched initializers are convincing, especially for JOSH3 on SLOPER4D and EMDB.
The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: contact-scene loss, contact-static loss, local human optimization, and focal-length optimization each have measurable effects.
The paper goes beyond offline optimization by showing that JOSH pseudo-labels can train an end-to-end model, JOSH3R, suggesting a plausible path toward scaling in-the-wild human-scene reconstruction.

The appendix provides important implementation details, broader comparisons, robustness checks under noisy initialization, and web-video labeling details, improving reproducibility relative to many submissions in this area.
weaknesses: The approach remains strongly dependent on off-the-shelf initialization quality, segmentation, contact prediction, and visible contact points. The stated limitations are real: failures in difficult contact, occlusion, weak scene visibility, or poor initialization could substantially degrade performance.

The main full 4D evaluation relies heavily on SLOPER4D, with only six public sequences, and the scene reconstruction evaluation excludes a difficult sequence. This weakens the claim that the method is broadly robust in unconstrained settings.

The strongest results combine very strong recent initializers such as VIMO and MASt3R, so part of the headline improvement comes from initialization quality. The matched-initializer comparisons help, but the paper could more cleanly separate gains from joint optimization versus gains from newer components.

The main baseline SynCHMR is reimplemented because the original code is unavailable. This is understandable, but it leaves some uncertainty about whether the comparison exactly matches the prior method.

JOSH is computationally expensive relative to feed-forward methods, and JOSH3R trades substantial accuracy for speed. The end-to-end model is promising but not yet consistently competitive across datasets, especially EMDB and RICH.

The web-video pseudo-labeling experiment is interesting but somewhat narrow: the videos appear focused on pedestrian street scenes, and the privacy/data filtering process is described only at a high level.
The code availability statement appears incomplete in the abstract and says release will occur upon publication, so reproducibility before acceptance is not fully established.
